grand_strategy.reading:
Georgia is run by a party that has decided its own survival, and a particular
idea of order, come before the country's formal strategy of Euro-Atlantic membership
(on paper still the constitutional line). Since the May 2024 foreign-influence law the
state has behaved as a hedging regime: it keeps every Western instrument it can without
paying the political price (candidate status, free trade, citizens' visa-free travel,
NATO contacts), keeps Russia calm (no sanctions, flights, trade, no talk of the
territories) and looks for other patrons (China, Turkey, Azerbaijan, the Gulf) and for a
different America. That is Luttwak's pattern of a move that works against its own end:
each step that protects power at home (the foreign-agents law, the arrests after
28 November 2024 and 4 October 2025, the party-ban case) lowers the value of the Western
shell that the economy rests on, and raises the weight of the one actor, Russia, whose
forces hold a fifth of the territory. Three signals that are not rows: the party ban was
widened to For Georgia in September-October 2026, a year after the first filing; Moscow
still says no dialogue without recognition of Abkhazia and South Ossetia; and a Hungarian
change of government in May 2026 reportedly removes the veto that protected Tbilisi from EU
sanctions. The Middle Corridor is the economic bet that holds the arrangement together:
cargo is up and the IMF sees 6.5% growth, but the corridor itself is not Georgia's to
secure, and its Western users are the ones being pushed away.

Direct Moscow-Sukhumi flights resumed in May 2025 over Georgian protests; a Russian-built customs terminal in Gali was reported in December 2025 and Kobakhidze denied Georgian involvement. Bond grievance: the 1992-93 war and its displacement. Mirrors the objective row.
